title: MEDI2004 W7 · Pharmacogenomics
subject: Pharmacology Fundamentals
content: Pharmacogenomics — how inherited genetic variation shapes drug response. Genetic factors account for 20–95% of the variability between patients, alongside disease state, age, gender, weight, diet and drug interactions. Raw material: mutations, polymorphisms (a variant carried by more than 1% of a population) and single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs). Pharmacogenetics classically means one gene; pharmacogenomics means genome-wide, though the terms are used interchangeably. Variation splits into pharmacodynamic (in the drug TARGET) and pharmacokinetic (in drug DISPOSITION). PD examples: the µ-opioid receptor A118G variant alters opioid response; VKORC1 variants change warfarin sensitivity, since warfarin's target is vitamin-K epoxide reductase. PK examples: CYP2D6 metaboliser phenotypes — poor, intermediate, normal and ultra-rapid. Codeine is a prodrug activated by CYP2D6 to morphine: poor metabolisers get little analgesia, while ultra-rapid metabolisers can suffer dangerous respiratory depression from a standard dose. Tamoxifen is a prodrug needing CYP2D6 to form active endoxifen; nortriptyline levels also track CYP2D6. P-glycoprotein (ABCB1) variants affect digoxin handling. The goal is precision medicine — read the genotype first, then match the right drug and dose to the right patient.

questions.question: Pharmacogenomics is the study of how a patient's drug response is shaped by their:
questions.explanation: Pharmacogenomics examines how inherited genetic variation affects the way a person responds to drugs.

questions.question: A single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) is a variation affecting:
questions.explanation: A SNP is a difference at a single nucleotide (DNA base) in the genome, the commonest form of genetic variation.

questions.question: Codeine only relieves pain well after it is converted by CYP2D6 into:
questions.explanation: Codeine is a prodrug; CYP2D6 converts it to morphine, the metabolite responsible for most of its analgesic effect.

questions.question: Precision (personalised) medicine aims to match the drug and dose to each patient's:
questions.explanation: Precision medicine uses a patient's genetic profile to choose the most effective and safest drug and dose.

questions.question: Roughly what share of the variability in drug response between patients is attributed to genetic factors?
questions.explanation: Genetic factors are estimated to account for 20–95% of between-patient variability, the largest single contributor.

questions.question: A CYP2D6 poor metaboliser given standard-dose codeine is most likely to experience:
questions.explanation: Poor metabolisers make little morphine from codeine, so they get inadequate analgesia at the usual dose.

questions.question: A CYP2D6 ultra-rapid metaboliser taking normal-dose codeine is at particular risk of:
questions.explanation: Ultra-rapid metabolisers convert codeine to morphine very quickly, so a standard dose can cause dangerous opioid toxicity.

questions.question: A genetic difference in a CYP450 enzyme that changes how fast a drug is cleared is a form of variation in:
questions.explanation: Variation in metabolising enzymes changes drug disposition (pharmacokinetics) — how the body handles the drug — rather than the target.

questions.question: A polymorphism in the µ-opioid receptor that changes a patient's response to morphine is variation in the:
questions.explanation: The receptor is the drug's target, so a variant there is pharmacodynamic variation — altering the effect for a given concentration.

questions.question: Variants in VKORC1 alter a patient's warfarin requirement because VKORC1 encodes warfarin's:
questions.explanation: Warfarin inhibits vitamin-K epoxide reductase (VKORC1); variants change target sensitivity, so the effective dose differs between patients.

questions.question: A genetic variant is formally called a polymorphism when it is present in a population at a frequency above:
questions.explanation: By convention a variant carried by more than 1% of a population is a polymorphism, distinguishing it from a rare mutation.

questions.question: Tamoxifen depends on CYP2D6 to form its active metabolite. Tamoxifen is therefore a:
questions.explanation: Tamoxifen must be metabolised by CYP2D6 to active endoxifen, so it is a prodrug whose benefit depends on that enzyme's activity.

questions.question: A breast-cancer patient who is a CYP2D6 poor metaboliser may get less benefit from tamoxifen because she forms less:
questions.explanation: CYP2D6 activates tamoxifen to endoxifen; poor metabolisers form less endoxifen, potentially reducing the drug's effectiveness.

questions.question: The term 'pharmacogenetics' classically refers to the effect on drug response of:
questions.explanation: Pharmacogenetics classically studies one gene's effect, whereas pharmacogenomics takes a genome-wide view; the terms now overlap.

questions.question: Variants in the ABCB1 gene affect digoxin levels because ABCB1 encodes the efflux transporter:
questions.explanation: ABCB1 encodes P-glycoprotein, which effluxes digoxin; variants change transport and hence plasma digoxin concentrations.

questions.question: Besides genetics, which factor also shifts an individual's response to a drug?
questions.explanation: Disease state such as liver dysfunction is one of several non-genetic factors — with age, weight, diet and interactions — that alter drug response.

questions.question: Compared with a polymorphism, a mutation is generally distinguished by being:
questions.explanation: A mutation is a less common change (typically under 1% frequency); once a variant becomes common it is termed a polymorphism.

questions.question: Why did regulators warn against giving codeine to some breastfeeding mothers who are ultra-rapid CYP2D6 metabolisers?
questions.explanation: Ultra-rapid metabolisers produce excess morphine, which can reach breast milk in amounts high enough to harm a nursing infant.

questions.question: For a drug that is INACTIVATED by CYP2D6 (not a prodrug), a poor metaboliser is most likely to show:
questions.explanation: If the enzyme normally clears the active drug, a poor metaboliser clears it slowly, so levels rise — the opposite of the prodrug case.

questions.question: A patient with a CYP2C9 variant that slows warfarin metabolism will generally need a warfarin dose that is:
questions.explanation: Slower metabolism raises warfarin exposure, so a lower dose achieves target anticoagulation and avoids bleeding.

questions.question: A patient clears a drug at a completely normal rate yet responds poorly to it. The most likely genetic explanation lies in the:
questions.explanation: Normal clearance points away from pharmacokinetics; poor response despite adequate levels suggests a variant in the drug's target (pharmacodynamic).

questions.question: The strongest argument for genotyping a patient BEFORE prescribing is that it can:
questions.explanation: Pre-treatment genotyping identifies patients at risk of poor response or toxicity before the drug is given, its key advantage over reacting afterwards.

questions.question: Two patients on the identical dose show opposite outcomes — one toxicity, one no effect. Pharmacogenomics attributes this chiefly to differences in their:
questions.explanation: Inherited variants in enzymes, transporters or targets can push two patients to opposite extremes on the same dose — the core lesson of the field.

questions.question: The µ-opioid receptor A118G variant is best classified as a source of variation in drug:
questions.explanation: A118G alters the receptor itself, so it changes the pharmacodynamic response to opioids rather than their pharmacokinetics.

questions.question: Genotyping CYP2D6 helps most for drugs that are:
questions.explanation: Only drugs metabolised by CYP2D6 are affected by its genotype; a drug cleared by other routes is unaffected by CYP2D6 status.

questions.question: For a prodrug activated by an enzyme, an ultra-rapid metaboliser phenotype tends to produce:
questions.explanation: Faster activation makes more of the active metabolite, which is why ultra-rapid metabolisers can overshoot with prodrugs like codeine.

questions.question: A study screening the entire genome for variants linked to a drug reaction is best described as:
questions.explanation: Surveying the whole genome is the pharmacogenomic (genome-wide) approach, broader than a classical single-gene pharmacogenetic test.
